text:
Anya: Quick RFC follow-up — sketched a different approach to burst credits that aggregates per-tenant unused headroom into a time-decayed shared pool for short spikes. Interested in tradeoffs.
Carl: Can you TL;DR the main difference from existing warmup-credit model? :thinking_face:
Anya: Today credits = reserved per-tenant tokens that expire. Proposal: tenants keep their baseline quota, plus we maintain a shared 'elastic credit pool' that accrues a fraction of unused reserved capacity each minute and decays over a configurable half-life.
Ben: So like interest-bearing credits? How do we prevent noisy tenants from draining the pool repeatedly?
Anya: Two parts: 1) per-tenant cooldown window after using shared credits, and 2) weighted decay so large tenants contribute/consume proportionally; also a short admission throttle that enforces burst-rate per-tenant.
Jamie: What about operator vs control-plane responsibilities? Which component tracks this pool?
Anya: Control plane keeps authoritative accounting and issues ephemeral tokens to the allocator. Operator only enforces node-level admission (accept/reject) based on token presented. This keeps orchestration centralized but execution local.
Carl: Sounds okay but worried about perf/latency on token issuance for high qps. Can we issue longer-lived ephemeral tokens and let allocator do local decrement?
Anya: Yes — token TTLs of 10s-60s depending on tenant SLO. Allocator can locally consume until TTL or local budget exhausted; then re-request. Reduces chattiness.
Ben: How do we measure fairness? If we weight by tenant size, big tenants still corner pool during system-wide spikes.
Anya: We'll combine three levers: proportional weight, a per-tenant max-share fraction, and an emergency cap that triggers fallback policies (preemptible shedding + model-fallback).
Jamie: Ops question: what observability surfaces do we need to be able to debug disagreements between control plane and operator?
Anya: Metrics: pool_size, per-tenant_contrib_rate, per-tenant_consumption_rate, token_issuance_latency, token_rejects, local_allocator_hits, token_ttl_expirations. Also audit log events: ISSUE/REVOKE/CONSUME for tokens.
SREBot: Deploy note: adding token endpoints will need rate-limits + auth. Consider mutual TLS and signing tokens (JWT) so allocators can validate without RPC.
Carl: JWT makes sense. What about clock skew across allocators and TTL enforcement?
Anya: Use monotonic counters per allocator and include issuance_time + issuer_id in token; allocator refuses tokens older than TTL + 2s. We already do similar for lease tokens.
Ben: Any simulation results? How much headroom can the shared pool realistically capture?
Anya: Ran a toy sim on 1k tenants: capturing ~12-18% of unused reserved capacity over 5m windows, reduces tail latency spikes by ~20% for moderate bursts. I'll upload sim code soon.
Jamie: Edge cases: node churn during a large drain — token revocation + graceful drain needed. We should allow allocator to redeem outstanding tokens during drain with a short grace.
Anya: Agreed. We'll add a REDEEM/DRAIN state that lets allocator report back consumed credit so control plane can reconcile.
Carl: OK — next steps? I can prototype token signing and TTL logic. Ben can run a more realistic sim with our production tenancy distribution. Jamie to draft metrics/alert deck.
Ben: On it. I'll try to model malicious/greedy tenants and failure modes.
Jamie: I'll update the runbook with emergency cap actions and observability ownership.
Anya: Thanks all — I'll post a short RFC doc with diagrams and the sim link. For now, feedback welcome in-thread. :thumbsup:
